name_en: Gui Hua Hong Cha (Osmanthus Black Tea)
processing: Black tea scented with fresh osmanthus flowers, layered over finished tea or added at a stage of processing; temperature and the flower-to-tea ratio are set by each producer.
harvest_season: The base tea is often picked in spring; flowers are gathered and scented in the autumn bloom, around October in Xianning.
appearance_dry: Dark twisted strands of black tea flecked with small golden-orange flowers.
appearance_liquor: Clear orange-red, as is typical of scented Chinese black teas.
appearance_wet: Reddish-brown leaf with softened flower pieces.
taste_profile: Sweet osmanthus sits over a mellow black tea, with a fine, smooth texture.

brewing.notes: Keep steeps short and do not oversteep: the flower aroma fades fast and the base tea can take over.

vintage_note: Sold by scenting season, usually the autumn bloom, on black tea from the same year when producers say so. Like other scented teas, it is best within about a year, since the flower aroma fades.
description:
Osmanthus black tea is a scented tea, not a place-bound appellation: black tea takes up the apricot-sweet smell of osmanthus flowers. It is made in more than one part of China, and Xianning in southern Hubei, which markets itself as China's osmanthus city, is a notable modern home for it.

The method varies. One Xianning producer spreads fresh flowers in layers over spring-made organic black tea; another adds them at different stages of black tea processing, adjusting heat and proportions. A published trial found that adding flowers during rolling gave a clear osmanthus aroma and sweet, mellow taste.

Brewed, it should smell of the flower first and then settle into a soft, sweet black tea. Short steeps keep it balanced. It works for people who find plain black tea a bit stern.

When buying, smell for real flowers rather than perfume, and ask for the scenting year. Good flower pieces are a pleasant sign, though they do not prove the tea was properly scented, and bags and flavoured versions are also sold under this name.
history:
As a Xianning product, this is recent work. One local team began research on osmanthus black tea in autumn 2018, and its processing code later became a Hubei local standard. Another producer, working with the city's agricultural research institute, started its own version in 2020.

Scenting tea with osmanthus is much older and widespread in China, but no specific origin for the black tea version is documented.
